newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS-Israel reform seeks convertible shekel soon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Israel reform seeks convertible shekel soon.

text.p: Israel's shekel will become fully convertible in international markets in a year under a currency reform agreed overnight, sources present at the decisive meeting said on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel also agreed to increase the amount institutional investors and businesses can invest abroad, the sources said.

The ceiling on overseas investment for institutionals, mainly provident funds, would rise to five percent of assets from the current two percent. Provident funds are popular savings schemes that enjoy special tax benefits.
At the same time taxes on real capital gains from overseas investments, currently at 35 percent, would be lowered though by how much has not yet been decided.
Restrictions on mutual funds -- such as limiting fund managers to no more than two funds investing in overseas shares -- would be abolished.
Netanyahu, Frenkel and Meridor also agreed to gradually raise the amount businesses can invest overseas.
Companies presently can invest abroad up to five percent of their total turnover or 10 percent of their capital, the larger of the two. This is likely to be raised to 25 percent for both.
The plan also would allow Israelis to send $10,000 a year to family members overseas, up from the present limit of $2,000.
Israelis will be able to open dollar accounts in Israeli or foreign banks in a year. At that point the remaining currency controls will be limited mainly to institutional investors.
